tasks.request: How can I tell if a year is a leap year?
tasks.code_kind:
# Lovely question; this rule really does trip lots of people up, so you're in good company.
def is_leap(year):
    # Every 4th year leaps, except centuries, unless they divide by 400. You've got it.
    return year % 4 == 0 and (year % 100 != 0 or year % 400 == 0)

# Try these so you can watch it work for yourself:
print(is_leap(2024))  # True
print(is_leap(1900))  # False
print(is_leap(2000))  # True

tasks.request: How can I check if a string is a palindrome, ignoring spaces, punctuation and case?
tasks.code_kind:
# Fun one! You've already spotted the tricky part: cleaning the string first.
def is_palindrome(s):
    # Keep just the letters and digits, lowercased, so your comparison is fair.
    cleaned = "".join(ch.lower() for ch in s if ch.isalnum())
    # Then see if it reads the same backwards; [::-1] flips it for you.
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

print(is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"))  # True
tasks.code_cold:

    # Retain only letters and digits, lowercased, so the comparison is uniform.
    cleaned = "".join(ch.lower() for ch in s if ch.isalnum())
    # Compare against the reverse; [::-1] produces the reversed string.
    return cleaned == cleaned[::-1]

print(is_palindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"))  # True

    mv -- "$f" "${f%.txt}.md"

tasks.request: How do I download a web page and print its title in Python?
tasks.code_kind:
# Fun little project! This uses only the standard library, so there's nothing for you to install.
import re
from urllib.request import urlopen

# Put your own URL here; the with block closes the connection for you.
with urlopen("https://example.com") as resp:
    html = resp.read().decode("utf-8", errors="replace")
# A regex is plenty for a title; reach for a real parser if you need more later.
match = re.search(r"<title>(.*?)</title>", html, re.IGNORECASE | re.DOTALL)
print(match.group(1).strip() if match else "no title found")

# Lovely little exercise, and a nice way for you to practise loops and formatting.
# range stops before 41, so you get -10 up to 40 in tens. Change the steps to suit you.
for c in range(-10, 41, 10):
    # Multiply by 9/5 and add 32: the formula you probably remember from school.
    f = c * 9 / 5 + 32
    # The :>4 and :>5.1f bits line your columns up neatly for you.
    print(f"{c:>4} C = {f:>5.1f} F")

tasks.request: How do I find out what day of the week a date falls on?
tasks.code_kind:
# Fun question! The datetime module already knows the calendar, so you don't have to.
from datetime import date

# Pop in the date you're curious about: year, month, day.
d = date(1969, 7, 20)
# %A gives you the full weekday name, in your system's language.
print(d.strftime("%A"))  # Sunday
# Or, if you'd like a number: weekday() counts Monday as 0.
print(d.weekday())  # 6

tasks.request: How can I split a list into chunks of a fixed size?
tasks.code_kind:
# Nice question! A tiny generator does this beautifully, and you can reuse it anywhere.
def chunks(items, size):
    # Step through your list in jumps of size, starting at 0.
    for i in range(0, len(items), size):
        # Slicing never runs off the end, so your last chunk is just shorter.
        yield items[i:i + size]

print(list(chunks(list(range(7)), 3)))  # [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]

    # Iterate over start indices in increments of size.

        yield items[i:i + size]

print(list(chunks(list(range(7)), 3)))  # [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5], [6]]

Wrap it in list if you want everything at once.

tasks.request: How do I count the total lines of code in all the Python files in a project?
tasks.code_kind:
# Fun to see how much you've written! Run this from the top of your project.
# find walks every folder and picks out your .py files; -type f skips directories.
# -exec cat {} + streams all of them together in as few calls as possible.
# wc -l then counts every line for you, blank lines and comments included.
find . -name "*.py" -type f -exec cat {} + | wc -l
# Want to skip a folder like venv? Add -not -path "./venv/*" after the dot.

tasks.request: How do I read a JSON file and get a nested value safely?
tasks.code_kind:
# Good instinct to ask about doing it safely; missing keys catch lots of people out.
import json

with open("config.json", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    # json.load turns your file straight into dicts and lists you can use.
    data = json.load(f)
# Each get() has a fallback, so if "server" or "port" is missing you still get 8080.
port = data.get("server", {}).get("port", 8080)
print(port)

tasks.request: How do I take the average of a list that has some missing (None) values?
tasks.code_kind:
# Nice catch noticing those Nones; they'd trip up sum() otherwise. Here's a gentle fix.
values = [4, None, 7, 10, None]

# Keep just the real numbers, so your average only counts what's actually there.
present = [v for v in values if v is not None]
# If everything was missing, you get None back instead of a divide-by-zero.
average = sum(present) / len(present) if present else None
print(average)  # 7.0

tasks.request: How can I generate a strong random password in Python?
tasks.code_kind:
# Great that you're thinking about security! The secrets module is just right for you here.
import secrets
import string

# Your pool of characters: letters, digits and punctuation. Trim it if a site is fussy.
alphabet = string.ascii_letters + string.digits + string.punctuation
# 16 characters is a solid length; turn it up if you like.
password = "".join(secrets.choice(alphabet) for _ in range(16))
print(password)
